content.p: Shortly before dawn on 28 September 1778, British soldiers crept into a cluster of barns and farmhouses at Old Tappan in Bergen County, New Jersey, and attacked a sleeping American cavalry detachment with the bayonet. The raid is known as the Baylor Massacre, after the American commander, Colonel George Baylor, and as the Tappan Massacre, after the place. Most of the men inside were killed, wounded or taken prisoner before they could fight back, and its conduct was controversial.

The town is now River Vale. The sources agree on the core facts: a surprise night attack, a bayonet assault on men who were asleep or bivouacked. They differ on the numbers and on the scale of the killing, and each figure below is given with the source that gave it.
content.h2: Why the dragoons were at Old Tappan
content.p: The 3rd Continental Light Dragoons were a mounted unit under Colonel George Baylor. Baylor had been a member of George Washington's staff from August 1775 until January 1777, when Washington gave him command of the 3rd Continental Dragoons. In the summer of 1778 the regiment was in Bergen County to keep an eye on the British army, which was then based around New York City and was seeking forage and provisions.

The Library of Virginia's biography of Baylor says that on the night of 27–28 September 1778 he was quartered with his troops at Old Tappan, about two and a half miles from the main army. The American Battlefield Trust adds that the Americans had moved the local livestock out of reach of the British before the dragoons settled into a series of barns and houses along Overkill Road. The Library of Virginia puts the quarters about two and a half miles from the main army.

The Revolutionary War Journal notes that Washington had sent a large body of Connecticut horse home in 1776, and that he soon found his army without the eyes and ears of a mobile force. The dragoons had been sent to the region to watch the British and strike at them when an opening appeared.
content.h2: A wider British sweep through Bergen County
content.p: The night attack at Old Tappan was one part of a larger British operation. The Journal of the American Revolution says that about 6,000 British and Provincial troops under Lieutenant General Lord Cornwallis entered Bergen County early on 22 September 1778 to gather forage and provisions for shipment down the Hackensack River to Manhattan. The British fanned out from the Hackensack to Fort Lee on the Hudson, with posts at New Bridge, Teaneck and Schraalenburgh.

The American forces in the area were small and scattered. The Journal lists a militia picket of about sixty men at the Liberty Pole, near modern Englewood, a New York militia company at Hackensack, the dragoons, and some New Jersey State troops under Major Peter Fell. On 23 September, 100 British cavalry swept the Liberty Pole picket away. The survivors crossed the Hackensack at New Bridge and joined Fell's troops and the New York militia, and the combined force moved north to Paramus with Baylor's cavalry.

A further militia unit, 350 men of the Orange County Militia from New York under Colonel Gilbert Cooper, took post at Tappan, within four miles of the advanced British pickets. The Journal says Cooper's men were collecting cattle from local inhabitants to keep it out of British hands. The British plan, as the Journal describes it, was to converge on both American forces. Cornwallis himself would march north from English Neighbourhood with about 2,500 men, a second column of about 1,000 men from the 71st Highlanders and the Loyalist Queen's Rangers would land behind the militia at Tappan, and Grey's column would come from the southwest.

The plan did not run to time. The Journal reports that the commander of the Highlanders and Provincials blamed the Royal Navy for slow river crossings. Lieutenant Colonel John Graves Simcoe of the Rangers wrote that the crossing to the west bank of the Hudson ran late, and that the timing of boat movements depends on tides and shoals. By the time the British reached Tappan, Cooper's militia had gone. The Journal reports an officer in Cornwallis's column writing that the 71st and Simcoe's corps "appear'd at Tapawn soon after we arrived there but met with nothing in their way."

While the main British column moved north, Grey's force struck the dragoons. The American Battlefield Trust says that with information provided by local Loyalists, the British under Major General Charles Grey quietly approached the American positions on the night of 27 September 1778. The Trust says the British did not fire a shot. They bayoneted the sleeping Continentals in the barns and residences.

The Revolutionary War Journal places the assault between two and three in the morning on 28 September. It describes the British vanguard first surprising the sergeant's guard, then the men silently surrounding the homes and barns where the Americans slept. Grey's men burst through the doors in a sudden rush. The Revolutionary War Journal says officers ordered the rank and file not to give quarter while unarmed men cried out for their lives.

The Journal of the American Revolution says that Grey's attack, with about 1,500 men, fell on 120 dragoons who were bivouacked. That is the figure the Journal gives; the Revolutionary War Journal puts the American force at about 105 men, and says the British side probably numbered about twice that when the two companies that opened the attack are counted. The sources do not agree on the size of either force, and this account uses the figures only as each source's own estimate.

Baylor was among the wounded. The Library of Virginia says he received a bayonet thrust in his lungs and was taken prisoner. The Journal of the American Revolution says the dragoons' major lay dead and their colonel was nearly so, and that the British took more than forty men prisoner. The Journal counts over twenty killed, a higher figure than the Revolutionary War Journal gives for the men in a single barn, which is discussed below.

The most direct record of the attack comes from the men who survived it. The Revolutionary War Journal quotes testimony gathered by Dr. David Griffith, surgeon of Woodford's Brigade, who treated the wounded and recorded what they said. One trooper, James Southward, is quoted as saying that the enemy entered the barn where his unit lay, that there were 13 men of the regiment in it, and that five of them were killed outright while the rest were bayoneted. He is also quoted as saying that he heard a British officer order his men to put all to death. The Journal reports that Southward had twelve wounds, ten of them in his breast, belly and back, and that most of the wounded later died.

The Revolutionary War Journal also quotes the same account to make a wider point: that very few or none of the British officers entered the American quarters to stop the attackers. The Journal's wording of this claim is strong.The American Battlefield Trust's biography of Grey takes a more cautious line, but it discusses the Paoli attack rather than Old Tappan: it says the Americans claimed British troops murdered unarmed prisoners there and labelled that engagement a massacre, and that the evidence for the claim is sparse.

The two accounts therefore differ on the scale of the killing and on the officers' conduct. The figure of five killed outright in one barn is Southward's own estimate as reported by the Revolutionary War Journal, and it is not a total for the attack. The Journal of the American Revolution's total of over twenty killed is not broken down by place. The Trust's account does not give a total at all.

A deserter's deposition also survives. The Journal of the American Revolution quotes one made on 29 September 1778 by Francis McCarny of the 37th Regiment, who said he deserted on the evening of 27 September and had told Colonel Cooper that the enemy were about to surprise him and Baylor's regiment. According to the same deposition, Cooper retired with his militia without warning Baylor. The Journal presents this as the reason the Americans were caught; it is McCarny's claim.

The Revolutionary War Journal also reports that in 1967 remains of soldiers were excavated near the Hackensack River at River Edge, New Jersey. Six bodies were found in three abandoned tanning vats from Haring's Tannery, and artifacts such as clothing remnants and buttons helped determine that they were American soldiers killed on the night of 28 September 1778.
content.h2: The tactic of the year before
content.p: The attack at Old Tappan was not the first of its kind. In September 1777, at Paoli in Pennsylvania, Grey had led a night assault on troops under General Anthony Wayne. The American Battlefield Trust describes the Paoli attack as a bayonet charge that Grey made after ordering his men to remove the flints from their muskets, so that a powder flash would not give away their position. Grey's men caught Wayne's troops off guard and smashed through them. The Trust says the nickname "No Flint" Grey came from that decision.

The Revolutionary War Journal argues that the Tappan attack followed the same pattern. Its vanguard surprised the sergeant's guard, and the men surrounded the buildings before bursting through the doors. The Revolutionary War Journal also notes that the Paoli action was dubbed a massacre, and that the Tappan attack was given the same label. The Trust, on the other hand, says the evidence that British troops murdered prisoners at Paoli is also thin. The word "massacre" is therefore a contested label in both cases, and the sources do not all use it in the same sense.

The Revolutionary War Journal notes that Wayne later used a night bayonet attack of his own, at Stony Point, New York, on 16 July 1779. It also says the British high command praised Wayne for sparing the garrison that threw down its weapons and called for mercy.

Charles Grey was born in 1729 into a Northumberland family, and he had already seen service in the Austrian Succession and Seven Years' Wars before 1777. The Encyclopedia of the American Revolution, hosted on Encyclopedia.com, says he fought at Minden and was wounded at Minden while serving as aide-de-camp to Prince Ferdinand. The American Battlefield Trust says Grey was controversial but that the controversies did nothing to affect his reputation in Britain.

After Old Tappan, Grey was criticised by Britons and Americans for allowing his men to commit atrocities, according to the Encyclopedia of the American Revolution. The same entry says Grey was unrepentant. He returned to England on 24 November 1778 and, in 1782, was promoted to lieutenant general and knighted. The Trust says King George granted him a knighthood in the Order of the Bath after his recall. He later became Governor of Guernsey, was made a baron in 1801, and was later created Viscount Howick and Earl Grey. He died in 1807.

George Baylor's life after the attack was shorter and quieter. The Library of Virginia says he married Lucy Page on 30 May 1778, a few months before the attack, and that the couple had two sons. While a prisoner he wrote to Washington on 19 October 1778 defending his conduct. Some of his fellow officers doubted that he had taken adequate precautions for the camp, but Washington never reprimanded him.

After his exchange, Baylor went back into the field with the 1st Continental Dragoons, which he led as colonel. His regiment guarded Congress in Philadelphia in October 1779, and the following December he was sent to the southern states, where he saw action in the last years of the war. The Library of Virginia says he still suffered from his wound but served through the end of the war and was promoted to brevet brigadier general on 30 September 1783. He left Virginia for Barbados in May 1784, in hopes of recovering his health. He died in Bridgetown on 9 November 1784 from complications of the old wound and was buried in the churchyard of Saint Michael's Cathedral.

The sources differ on the number of men involved and on the outcome. The Journal of the American Revolution gives the British force as about 1,500 and the American force as 120 dragoons. The Revolutionary War Journal gives about 105 Americans, and says the attackers were probably about double that figure. Neither source gives an exact count of the British troops who took part.

They also differ on the casualties. The Journal of the American Revolution counts over twenty men killed and more than forty captured. The Revolutionary War Journal reports five killed outright in the barn described in Southward's testimony and says most of the wounded later died. Its overall count, which it treats as the accepted one, is 69 casualties in all: 15 dead, and 54 others wounded or captured. The Library of Virginia's biography says Baylor was quartered with his troops when the attack came, and it does not say whether any of the officers were absent that night.

The sources also disagree on the place. The American Battlefield Trust and the Journal of the American Revolution place the attack at Old Tappan, and the Journal says the place is now River Vale, New Jersey. The Library of Virginia's biography calls it Old Tappan, New York.

Finally, the sources differ on the date of the Paoli attack that Grey made before Old Tappan. The Revolutionary War Journal gives 20 September 1777, while the Encyclopedia of the American Revolution gives 21 September. The attack at Old Tappan itself is dated to the night of 27 September and the early hours of 28 September across the sources.
